entries.0331a4bd318a93f68478746819874e8ff265c805: <div sID="gen33174" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="Heb.13" sID="Heb.13"/> <div eID="gen33174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33175" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33176" type="x-p"/> The apostle, having treated largely of Christ, and faith, and free grace, and gospel privileges, and warned the Hebrews against apostasy, now, in the close of all, recommends several excellent duties to them, as the proper fruits of faith (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.1-Heb.13.17">ver. 1-17</reference>); he then bespeaks their prayers for him, and offers up his prayers to God for them, gives them some hope of seeing himself and Timothy, and ends with the general salutation and benediction, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.18-Heb.13.25">ver. 18, to the end</reference>.
entries.f2e8ecf2c8d91a8652c8c98fa60a4584b789de14: <div eID="gen33176" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33175" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Various Duties. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen33177" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Let brotherly love continue. <hi type="super">2</hi> Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares. <hi type="super">3</hi> Remember them that are in bonds, as bound with them; <hi type="italic">and</hi> them which suffer adversity, as being yourselves also in the body. <hi type="super">4</hi> Marriage <hi type="italic">is</hi> honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge. <hi type="super">5</hi> <hi type="italic">Let your</hi> conversation <hi type="italic">be</hi> without covetousness; <hi type="italic">and be</hi> content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee. <hi type="super">6</hi> So that we may boldly say, The Lord <hi type="italic">is</hi> my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me. <hi type="super">7</hi> Remember them which have the rule over you, who have spoken unto you the word of God: whose faith follow, considering the end of <hi type="italic">their</hi> conversation. <hi type="super">8</hi> Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever. <hi type="super">9</hi> Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. For <hi type="italic">it is</hi> a good thing that the heart be established with grace; not with meats, which have not profited them that have been occupied therein. <hi type="super">10</hi> We have an altar, whereof they have no right to eat which serve the tabernacle. 11 For the bodies of those beasts, whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by the high priest for sin, are burned without the camp. <hi type="super">12</hi> Wherefore Jesus also, that he might sanctify the people with his own blood, suffered without the gate. <hi type="super">13</hi> Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp, bearing his reproach. <hi type="super">14</hi> For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come. <hi type="super">15</hi> By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of <hi type="italic">our</hi> lips giving thanks to his name. <hi type="super">16</hi> But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased. <hi type="super">17</hi> Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that <hi type="italic">is</hi> unprofitable for you. <div eID="gen33177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33178" type="x-p"/> The design of Christ in giving himself for us is that he may purchase <hi type="italic">to himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.</hi> Now the apostle calls the believing Hebrews to the performance of many excellent duties, in which it becomes Christians to excel. <div eID="gen33178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33179" type="x-p"/> I. To brotherly love (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.1">v. 1</reference>), by which he does not only mean a general affection to all men, as our brethren by nature, all made of the same blood, nor that more limited affection which is due to those who are of the same immediate parents, but that special and spiritual affection which ought to exist among the children of God. 1. It is here supposed that the Hebrews had this love one for another. Though, at this time, that nation was miserably divided and distracted among themselves, both about matters of religion and the civil state, yet there was true brotherly love left among those of them who believed on Christ; and this appeared in a very eminent manner presently after the shedding forth of the Holy Ghost, when they had all things common, and sold their possessions to make a general fund of subsistence to their brethren. The spirit of Christianity is a spirit of love. Faith works by love. The true religion is the strongest bond of friendship; if it be not so, it has its name for nothing. 2. This brotherly love was in danger of being lost, and that in a time of persecution, when it would be most necessary; it was in danger of being lost by those disputes that were among them concerning the respect they ought still to have to the ceremonies of the Mosaic law. Disputes about religion too often produce a decay of Christian affection; but this must be guarded against, and all proper means used to preserve brotherly love. Christians should always love and live as brethren, and the more they grow in devout affection to God their heavenly Father the more they will grow in love to one another for his sake. <div eID="gen33179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33180" type="x-p"/> II. To hospitality: <hi type="italic">Be not forgetful to entertain strangers for his sake,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.2">v. 2</reference>. We must add to brotherly kindness charity. Here observe, 1. The duty required—<hi type="italic">to entertain strangers,</hi> both those that are strangers to the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to our persons, especially those who know themselves to be strangers here and are seeking another country, which is the case of the people of God, and was so at this time: the believing Jews were in a desperate and distressed condition. But he seems to speak of strangers as such; though we know not who they are, nor whence they come, yet, seeing they are without any certain dwelling place, we should allow them room in our hearts and in our houses, as we have opportunity and ability. 2. The motive: <hi type="italic">Thereby some have entertained angels unawares;</hi> so Abraham did (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.1-Gen.18.32">Gen. xviii.</reference>), and Lot (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.1-Gen.19.38">Gen. xix.</reference>), and one of those that Abraham entertained was the Son of God; and, though we cannot suppose this will ever be our case, yet what we do to strangers, in obedience to him, he will reckon and reward as done to himself. <reference osisRef="Matt.25.35">Matt. xxv. 35</reference>, <hi type="italic">I was a stranger, and you took me in.</hi> God has often bestowed honours and favours upon his hospitable servants, beyond all their thoughts, <hi type="italic">unawares.</hi> <div eID="gen33180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33181" type="x-p"/> III. To Christian sympathy: <hi type="italic">Remember those that are in bonds,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.3">v. 3</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen33181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33182" type="x-p"/> 1. The duty—to <hi type="italic">remember those that are in bonds</hi> and in <hi type="italic">adversity.</hi> (1.) God often orders it so that while some Christians and churches are in adversity others enjoy peace and liberty. All are not called at the same time to resist unto blood. (2.) Those that are themselves at liberty must sympathize with those that are in bonds and adversity, as if they were bound with them in the same chain: they must fell the sufferings of their brethren. <div eID="gen33182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33183" type="x-p"/> 2. The reason of the duty: <hi type="italic">As being yourselves in the body;</hi> not only in the body natural, and so liable to the like sufferings, and you should sympathize with them now that others may sympathize with you when your time of trial comes; but in the same mystical body, under the same head, <hi type="italic">and if one member suffer all the rest suffer with it,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.26">1 Cor. xii. 26</reference>. It would be unnatural in Christians not to bear each other's burdens. <div eID="gen33183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33184" type="x-p"/> IV. To purity and chastity, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.4">v. 4</reference>. Here you have, 1. A recommendation of God's ordinance of marriage, that it <hi type="italic">is honourable in all,</hi> and ought to be so esteemed by all, and not denied to those to whom God has not denied it. It is honourable, for God instituted it for man in paradise, knowing it was not good for him to be alone. He married and blessed the first couple, the first parents of mankind, to direct all to look unto God in that great concern, and to marry in the Lord. Christ honoured marriage with his presence and first miracle. It is honourable as a means to prevent impurity and a defiled bed. It is <hi type="italic">honourable</hi> and happy, when persons come together pure and chaste, and preserve the marriage bed undefiled, not only from unlawful but inordinate affections. 2. A dreadful but just censure of impurity and lewdness: <hi type="italic">Whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.</hi> (1.) God knows who are guilty of such sins, no darkness can hide them from him. (2.) He will call such sins by their proper names, not by the names of love and gallantry, but of whoredom and adultery, whoredom in the single state and adultery in the married state. (3.) He will bring them into judgment, he will judge them, either by their own consciences here, and <hi type="italic">set their sins in order before them</hi> for their deep humiliation (and conscience, when awakened, will be very severe upon such sinners), or he will set them at his tribunal at death, and in the last day; he will convict them, condemn them, and cast them out for ever, if they die under the guilt of this sin. <div eID="gen33184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33185" type="x-p"/> V. To Christian contentment, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.5-Heb.13.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Here observe, 1. The sin that is contrary to this grace and duty—<hi type="italic">covetousness,</hi> an over eager desire of the wealth of this world, envying those who have more than we. This sin we must allow no place in our conversation; for, though it be a secret lust lurking in the heart, if it be not subdued it will enter into our conversation, and discover itself in our manner of speaking and acting. We must take care not only to keep this sin down, but to root it out of our souls. 2. The duty and grace that is contrary to covetousness—being satisfied and pleased <hi type="italic">with such things as we have;</hi> present things, for past things cannot be recalled, and future things are only in the hand of God. What God gives us from day to day we must be content with, though it fall short of what we have enjoyed heretofore, and though it do not come up to our expectations for the future. We must be content with our present lot. We must bring our minds to our present condition, and this is the sure way to contentment; and those who cannot do it would not be contented though God should raise their condition to their minds, for the mind would rise with the condition. Haman was the great court-favourite, and yet not contented—Ahab on the throne, and yet not contented—Adam in paradise, and yet not contented; yea, the angels in heaven, and yet not contented; but Paul, though abased and empty, had <hi type="italic">learned in</hi> every <hi type="italic">state, in</hi> any <hi type="italic">state, therewith to be content.</hi> 3. What reason Christians have to be contented with their lot. (1.) <hi type="italic">God hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.5-Heb.13.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. This was said to Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.5">ch. i. 5</reference>), but belongs to all the faithful servants of God. Old-Testament promises may be applied to New-Testament saints. This promise contains the sum and substance of all the promises. <hi type="italic">I will never,</hi> no, <hi type="italic">never leave thee, nor</hi> ever <hi type="italic">forsake thee.</hi> Here are no fewer than five negatives heaped together, to confirm the promise; the true believer shall have the gracious presence of God with him in life, at death, and for ever. (2.) From this comprehensive promise they may assure themselves of help from God: <hi type="italic">So that we may boldly say, The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man shall do unto me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.6">v. 6</reference>. Men can do nothing against God, and God can make all that men do against his people to turn to their good. <div eID="gen33185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33186" type="x-p"/> VI. To the duty Christians owe to their ministers, and that both to those that are dead and to those that are yet alive. <div eID="gen33186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33187" type="x-p"/> 1. To those that are dead: <hi type="italic">Remember those that have had the rule over you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.7">v. 7</reference>. Here observe, <div eID="gen33187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33188" type="x-p"/> (1.) The description given of them. They were such as had the rule over them, and had spoken to them the word of God; their guides and governors, who had spoken to them the word of God. Here is the dignity to which they were advanced—to be rulers and leaders of the people, not according to their own will, but the will and word of God; and this character they filled up with suitable duty: they did not rule at a distance, and rule by others, but they ruled by personal presence and instruction, according to the word of God. <div eID="gen33188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33189" type="x-p"/> (2.) The duties owing to them, even when they were dead. <div eID="gen33189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33190" type="x-p"/> [1.] "<hi type="italic">Remember them</hi>—their preaching, their praying, their private counsel, their example." <div eID="gen33190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33191" type="x-p"/> [2.] "<hi type="italic">Follow</hi> their <hi type="italic">faith;</hi> be stedfast in the profession of the faith they preached to you, and labour after the grace of faith by which they lived and died so well. <hi type="italic">Consider the end of their conversation,</hi> how quickly, how comfortably, how joyfully, they finished their course!" Now this duty of following the same true faith in which they had been instructed the apostle enlarges much upon, and presses them earnestly to it, not only from the remembrance of their faithful deceased guides, but from several other motives. <div eID="gen33191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33192" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> From the immutability and eternity of the Lord Jesus Christ. Though their ministers were some dead, others dying, yet the great head and high priest of the church, <hi type="italic">the bishop of their souls,</hi> ever lives, and is ever the same; and they should be stedfast and immovable, in imitation of Christ, and should remember that Christ ever lives to observe and reward their faithful adherence to his truths, and to observe and punish their sinful departure from him. Christ is the same in the Old-Testament day, in the gospel day, and will be so to his people for ever. <div eID="gen33192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33193" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> From the nature and tendency of those erroneous doctrines that they were in danger of falling in with. <div eID="gen33193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33194" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">a.</hi> They were divers and various (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.9">v. 9</reference>), different from what they had received from their former faithful teachers, and inconsistent with themselves. <div eID="gen33194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33195" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">b.</hi> They were strange doctrines: such as the gospel church was unacquainted with foreign to the gospel. <div eID="gen33195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33196" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">c.</hi> They were of an unsettling, distracting nature, like the wind by which the ship is tossed, and in danger of being driven from its anchor, carried away, and split upon the rocks. They were quite contrary to that grace of God which fixes and establishes the heart, which is an excellent thing. These strange doctrines keep the heart always fluctuating and unsettled. <div eID="gen33196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33197" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">d.</hi> They were mean and low as to their subject. They were about external, little, perishing things, such as <hi type="italic">meats and drinks,</hi> &c. <div eID="gen33197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33198" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">e.</hi> They were unprofitable. Those who were most taken with them, and employed about them, got no real good by them to their own souls. They did not make them more holy, nor more humble, nor more thankful, nor more heavenly. <div eID="gen33198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33199" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">f.</hi> They would exclude those who embraced them from the privileges of the Christian altar (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">We have an altar.</hi> This is an argument of the great weight, and therefore the apostle insists the longer upon it. Observe, <div eID="gen33199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33200" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">a.</hi>) The Christian church has its altar. It was objected against the primitive Christians that their assemblies were destitute of an altar; but this was not true. <hi type="italic">We have an alter,</hi> not a material altar, but a personal one, and that is Christ; he is both our altar, and our sacrifice; he sanctifies the gift. The altars under the law were types of Christ; the brazen altar of the sacrifice, the golden altar of his intercession. <div eID="gen33200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33201" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">b.</hi>) This altar furnishes out a feast for true believers, a feast upon the sacrifice, a <hi type="italic">feast of fat things,</hi> spiritual strength and growth, and holy delight and pleasure. The Lord's table is not our altar, but it is furnished with provision from the altar. <hi type="italic">Christ our passover is sacrificed for us</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.7">1 Cor. v. 7</reference>), and it follows, <hi type="italic">therefore let us keep the feast.</hi> The Lord's supper is the feast of the gospel passover. <div eID="gen33201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33202" type="x-p"/> (<hi type="italic">c.</hi>) Those who adhere to the tabernacle or the Levitical dispensation, or return to it again, exclude themselves from the privileges of this altar, from the benefits purchased by Christ. If they serve the tabernacle, they are resolved to subject themselves to antiquated rites and ceremonies, to renounce their right to the Christian altar; and this part of the argument he first proves and then improves. <div eID="gen33202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33203" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">a.</hi>] He proves that this servile adherence to the Jewish state is a bar to the privileges of the gospel altar; and he argues thus:—Under the Jewish law, no part of the sin-offering was to be eaten, but all must be burnt without the camp while they dwelt in tabernacles, and without the gates when they dwelt in cities: now, if they will still be subject to that law, they cannot eat at the gospel-altar; for that which is eaten there is furnished from Christ, who is the great sin-offering. Not that it is the very sin-offering itself, as the papists affirm; for then it was not to be eaten, but burnt; but the gospel feast is the fruit and procurement of the sacrifice, which those have no right to who do not acknowledge the sacrifice itself. And that it might appear that Christ was really the antitype of the sin-offering, and, as such, might sanctify or cleanse his people with his own blood, he conformed himself to the type, in suffering without the gate. This was a striking specimen of his humiliation, as if he had not been fit either for sacred or civil society! And this shows how sin, which was the meritorious cause of the sufferings of Christ, is a forfeiture of all sacred and civil rights, and the sinner a common plague and nuisance to all society, if God should be strict to mark iniquity. Having thus shown that adherence to the Levitical law would, even according to its own rules, debar men from the Christian altar, he proceeds, <div eID="gen33203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33204" type="x-p"/> [<hi type="italic">b.</hi>] To improve this argument (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.13-Heb.13.15">v. 13-15</reference>) in suitable advices. <hi type="italic">First, Let us go forth therefore unto him without the camp;</hi> go forth from the ceremonial law, from sin, from the world, from ourselves, our very bodies, when he calls us. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Let us be willing to <hi type="italic">bear his reproach,</hi> be willing to be accounted the offscouring of all things, not worthy to live, not worthy to die a common death. This was his reproach, and we must submit to it; and we have the more reason because, whether we go forth from this world to Christ or no, we must necessarily go forth in a little time by death; for <hi type="italic">here we have no continuing city.</hi> Sin, sinners, death, will not suffer us to continue long here; and therefore we should go forth now by faith, and seek in Christ the rest and settlement which this world cannot afford us, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.14">v. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Let us make a right use of this altar; not only partake of the privileges of it, but discharge the duties of the altar, as those whom Christ has made priests to attend on this altar. Let us bring our sacrifices to this altar, and to this our high priest, and offer them up by him, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.15-Heb.13.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. Now what are the sacrifices which we must bring and offer on this altar, even Christ? Not any expiatory sacrifices; there is no need of them. Christ has offered the great <hi type="italic">sacrifice of atonement,</hi> ours are only the sacrifices of acknowledgment; and they are, 1. The sacrifice of praise to God, which we should offer up to God continually. In this are included all adoration and prayer, as well as thanksgiving; this is <hi type="italic">the fruit of our lips;</hi> we must speak forth the praises of God from unfeigned lips; and this must be offered only to God, not to angels, nor saints, nor any creature, but to the name of God alone; and it must be by Christ, in a dependence upon his meritorious satisfaction and intercession. 2. The sacrifice of alms-deeds, and Christian charity: <hi type="italic">To do good, and to communicate, forget now; for with such sacrifices God is well pleased,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.13.16">v. 16</reference>. We must, according to our power, <hi type="italic">communicate</hi> to the necessities of the souls and bodies of men; not contenting ourselves to offer the sacrifice of our lips, mere words, but the sacrifice of good deeds; and these we must lay down upon this altar, not depending upon the merit of our good deeds, but of our great high priest; and with such sacrifices as these, adoration and alms thus offered up, God is well pleased; he will accept the offering with pleasure, and will accept and bless the offers through Christ. <div eID="gen33204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33205" type="x-p"/> 2. Having thus told us the duty Christians owe to their deceased ministers, which principally consists in following their faith and not departing from it, the apostle tells us what is the duty that people owe to their living ministers (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">v. 17</reference>) and the reasons of that duty: (1.) The duty—to obey them, and submit themselves to them. It is not an implicit obedience, or absolute submission, that is here required, but only so far as is agreeable to the mind and will of God revealed in his word; and yet it is truly obedience and submission, and that not only to God, but to the authority of the ministerial office, which is of God as certainly, in all things belonging to that office, as the authority of parents or of civil magistrates in the things within their sphere. Christians must submit to be instructed by their ministers, and not think themselves too wise, too good, or too great, to learn from them; and, when they find that ministerial instructions are agreeable to the written word, they must obey them. (2.) The motives to this duty. [1.] They have the rule over the people; their office, though not magisterial, yet is truly authoritative. They have no authority to lord it over the people, but to lead them in the ways of God, by informing and instructing them, explaining the word of God to them, and applying it to their several cases. They are not to make laws of their own, but to interpret the laws of God; nor is their interpretation to be immediately received without examination, but the people must search the scriptures, and so far as the instructions of their minister are according to that rule they ought to receive them, <hi type="italic">not as the word of men, but, as they are indeed, the word of God, that works effectually in those that believe.</hi> [2.] They watch for the souls of the people, not to ensnare them, but to save them; to gain them, not to themselves, but to Christ; to build them up in knowledge, faith, and holiness. They are to watch against every thing that may be hurtful to the souls of men, and to give them warning of dangerous errors, of the devices of Satan, of approaching judgments; they are to watch for all opportunities of helping the souls of men forward in the way to heaven. [3.] They must give an account how they have discharged their duty, and what has become of the souls committed to their trust, whether any have been lost through their neglect, and whether any of them have been brought in and built up under their ministry. [4.] They would be glad to give a good account of themselves and their hearers. If they can then give in an account of their own fidelity and success, it will be a joyful day to them; those souls that have been converted and confirmed under their ministry <hi type="italic">will be their joy, and their crown, in the day of the Lord Jesus.</hi> [5.] If they give up their account with grief, it will be the people's loss as well as theirs. It is the interest of hearers that the account their ministers give of them may be with joy, and not with grief. If faithful ministers be not successful, the grief will be theirs, but the loss will be the people's. Faithful ministers have delivered their own souls, but a fruitless and faithless people's blood and ruin will be upon their own heads.
entries.c47b397c0a81b20fe77f50a57deae54ea6693f1c: <div eID="gen33205" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Conclusion. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 62.)</title> <div sID="gen33206" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> Pray for us: for we trust we have a good conscience, in all things willing to live honestly. <hi type="super">19</hi> But I beseech <hi type="italic">you</hi> the rather to do this, that I may be restored to you the sooner. <hi type="super">20</hi> Now the God of peace, that brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant, <hi type="super">21</hi> Make you perfect in every good work to do his will, working in you that which is wellpleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ; to whom <hi type="italic">be</hi> glory for ever and ever. Amen. <hi type="super">22</hi> And I beseech you, brethren, suffer the word of exhortation: for I have written a letter unto you in few words. <hi type="super">23</hi> Know ye that <hi type="italic">our</hi> brother Timothy is set at liberty; with whom, if he come shortly, I will see you. <hi type="super">24</hi> Salute all them that have the rule over you, and all the saints. They of Italy salute you. <hi type="super">25</hi> Grace <hi type="italic">be</hi> with you all. Amen. <div eID="gen33206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33207" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The apostle recommends himself, and his fellow-sufferers, to the prayers of the Hebrew believers (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Pray for us;</hi> for me and Timothy" (mentioned <reference osisRef="Heb.13.23">v. 23</reference>), "and for all those of us who labour in the ministry of the gospel." <div eID="gen33207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33208" type="x-p"/> 1. This is one part of the duty which people owe to their ministers. Ministers need the prayers of the people; and the more earnestly the people pray for their ministers the more benefit they may expect to reap from their ministry. They should pray that God would teach those who are to teach them, that he would make them vigilant, and wise, and zealous, and successful—that he would assist them in all their labours, support them under all their burdens, and strengthen them under all their temptations. <div eID="gen33208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33209" type="x-p"/> 2. There are good reasons why people should pray for their ministers; he mentions two:— <div eID="gen33209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33210" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">We trust we have a good conscience,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Heb.13.18">v. 18</reference>. Many of the Jews had a bad opinion of Paul, because he, being a Hebrew of the Hebrews, had cast off the Levitical law and preached up Christ: now he here modestly asserts his own integrity: <hi type="italic">We trust we have a good conscience, in all things willing to live honestly. We trust!</hi> he might have said, <hi type="italic">We know;</hi> but he chose to speak in a humble style, to teach us all not to be too confident of ourselves, but to maintain a godly jealousy over our own hearts. "We trust we have a <hi type="italic">good conscience,</hi> an enlightened and well-informed conscience, a clean and pure conscience, a tender and faithful conscience, a conscience testifying for us, not against us: a good conscience <hi type="italic">in all things,</hi> in the duties both of the first and second table, towards God and towards men, and especially in all things pertaining to our ministry; we would act honestly and sincerely in all things." Observe, [1.] A good conscience has a respect to all God's commands and all our duty. [2.] Those who have this good conscience, yet need the prayers of others. [3.] Conscientious ministers are public blessings, and deserve the prayers of the people. <div eID="gen33210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33211" type="x-p"/> (2.) Another reason why he desires their prayers is that he hoped thereby to be the sooner restored to them (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.19">v. 19</reference>), intimating that he had been formerly among them,—that, now he was absent from them, he had a great desire and real intention to come again to them,—and that the best way to facilitate his return to them, and to make it a mercy to him and them, was to make it a matter of their prayer. When ministers come to a people as a return of prayer, they come with greater satisfaction to themselves and success to the people. We should fetch in all our mercies by prayer. <div eID="gen33211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33212" type="x-p"/> II. He offers up his prayers to God for them, being willing to do for them as he desired they should do for him: <hi type="italic">Now the God of peace,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Heb.13.20">v. 20</reference>. In this excellent prayer observe, 1. The title given to God—<hi type="italic">the God of peace,</hi> who was found out a way for peace and reconciliation between himself and sinners, and who loves peace on earth and especially in his churches. 2. The great work ascribed to him: <hi type="italic">He hath brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus,</hi> &c. Jesus raised himself by his own power; and yet the Father was concerned in it, attesting thereby that justice was satisfied and the law fulfilled. He rose again for our justification; and that divine power by which he was raised is able to do every thing for us that we stand in need of. 3. The titles given to Christ—our Lord Jesus, our sovereign, our Saviour, and the great shepherd of the sheep, promised in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Isa. xl. 11</reference>, declared by himself to be so, <reference osisRef="John.10.14-John.10.15">John x. 14, 15</reference>. Ministers are under-shepherds, Christ is the great shepherd. This denotes his interest in his people. They are the flock of his pasture, and his care and concern are for them. He feeds them, and leads them, and watches over them. 4. The way and method in which God is reconciled, and Christ raised from the dead: <hi type="italic">Through the blood of the everlasting covenant.</hi> The blood of Christ satisfied divine justice, and so procured Christ's release from the prison of the grace, as having paid our debt, according to an eternal covenant or agreement between the Father and the Son; and this blood is the sanction and seal of an everlasting covenant between God and his people. 5. The mercy prayed for: <hi type="italic">Make you perfect in every good work,</hi> &c., <reference osisRef="Heb.13.21">v. 21</reference>. Observe, (1.) The perfection of the saints in every good work is the great thing desired by them and for them, that they may here have a perfection of integrity, a clear mind, a clean heart, lively affections, regular and resolved wills, and suitable strength for every good work to which they are called now, and at length a perfection of degrees to fit them for the employment and felicity of heaven. (2.) The way in which God makes his people perfect; it is by working in them always what is pleasing in his sight, and that <hi type="italic">through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever.</hi> Observe, [1.] There is no good thing wrought in us but it is the work of God; he works in us, before we are fit for any good work. [2.] No good thing is wrought in us by God, but through Jesus Christ, for his sake and by his Spirit. And therefore, [3.] Eternal glory is due to him, who is the cause of all the good principles wrought in us and all the good works done by us. To this every one should say, <hi type="italic">Amen.</hi> <div eID="gen33212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33213" type="x-p"/> III. He gives the Hebrews an account of Timothy's liberty and his hopes of seeing them with him in a little time, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.23">v. 23</reference>. It seems, Timothy had been a prisoner, doubtless for the gospel, but now he was set at liberty. The imprisonment of faithful ministers is an honour to them, and their enlargement is matter of joy to the people. He was pleased with the hopes of not only seeing Timothy, but seeing the Hebrews with him. Opportunities of writing to the churches of Christ are desired by the faithful ministers of Christ, and pleasant to them. <div eID="gen33213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33214" type="x-p"/> IV. Having given a brief account of this his letter, and begged their attention to it (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.22">v. 22</reference>), he closes with salutations, and a solemn, though short benediction. <div eID="gen33214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33215" type="x-p"/> 1. The salutation. (1.) From himself to them, directed to all their ministers who had rule over them, and to all the saints; to them all, ministers and people. (2.) From the Christians in Italy to them. It is a good thing to have the law of holy love and kindness written in the hearts of Christians one towards another. Religion teaches men the truest civility and good-breeding. It is not a sour nor morose thing. <div eID="gen33215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33216" type="x-p"/> 2. The solemn, though short benediction (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.25">v. 25</reference>): <hi type="italic">Grace be with you all. Amen.</hi> Let the favour of God be towards you, and his grace continually working in you, and with you, bringing forth the fruits of holiness, as the first-fruits of glory. When the people of God have been conversing together by word or writing, it is good to part with prayer, desiring for each other the continuance of the gracious presence of God, that they may meet together again in the world of praise.  <chapter eID="Heb.13"/> <div eID="gen33216" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen32737" osisID="Heb" type="book"/>

entries.5e37d2bfd70c4bd597629075c263bfecf2839a9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18596"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Heb.13.1-Heb.13.25">He 13:1-25</reference>. Exhortation to Various Graces, Especially Constancy in Faith, Following Jesus amidst Reproaches. Conclusion, with Pieces of Intelligence and Salutations.</title> <div sID="gen39262" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18596"/><hi type="bold">1. brotherly love--</hi>a distinct special manifestation of "charity" or "love" (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.7">2Pe 1:7</reference>). The Church of Jerusalem, to which in part this Epistle was addressed, was distinguished by this grace, we know from Acts (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.6.10">He 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.32-Heb.10.34">10:32-34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.12">12:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen39262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">continue--</hi>Charity will itself continue. See that it continue with you. <div eID="gen39263" type="x-p"/>
entries.7287d0c96b83819213a5dbb0453af0642ceaf23b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18598"/><div sID="gen39267" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18598"/><hi type="bold">3. Remember--</hi>in prayers and acts of kindness.<div eID="gen39267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39268" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bound with them--</hi>by virtue of the unity of the members in the body under one Head, Christ (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.26">1Co 12:26</reference>).<div eID="gen39268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39269" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">suffer adversity--</hi>Greek, "are in evil state."<div eID="gen39269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39270" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">being yourselves also in the body--</hi>and so liable to the adversities incident to the natural body, which ought to dispose you the more to sympathize with them, not knowing how soon your own turn of suffering may come. "One experiences adversity almost his whole life, as Jacob; another in youth, as Joseph; another in manhood, as Job; another in old age" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen39270" type="x-p"/>
entries.36d153cfd7e24019b5b71aaa40a19210f7ec821f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18599"/><div sID="gen39271" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18599"/><hi type="bold">4. is, &c.--</hi>Translate, "Let marriage be treated as honorable": as <reference osisRef="Heb.13.5">He 13:5</reference> also is an exhortation.<div eID="gen39271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in all--</hi>"in the case of all men": "among all." "To avoid fornication let EVERY MAN have his own wife" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.2">1Co 7:2</reference>). Judaism and Gnosticism combined were soon about to throw discredit on marriage. The venerable Paphnutius, in the Council of Nice, quoted this verse for the justification of the married state. If one does not himself marry, he should not prevent others from doing so. Others, especially Romanists, translate, "in all things," as in <reference osisRef="Heb.13.18">He 13:18</reference>. But the warning being against lasciviousness, the contrast to "whoremongers and adulterers" in the parallel clause, requires the "in all" in this clause to refer to persons.<div eID="gen39272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39273" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the bed undefiled--</hi>Translate, as Greek requires "undefiled" to be a predicate, not an epithet, "And let the bed be undefiled."<div eID="gen39273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39274" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God will judge--</hi>Most whoremongers escape the notice of human tribunals; but God takes particular cognizance of those whom man does not punish. Gay immoralities will then be regarded in a very different light from what they are now. <div eID="gen39274" type="x-p"/>
entries.8c017f9d66cfe68d6df4d338628b4d49a8105847: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18600"/><div sID="gen39275" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18600"/><hi type="bold">5. conversation--</hi>"manner of life." The love of filthy lust and the love of filthy lucre follow one another as closely akin, both alienating the heart from the Creator to the creature.<div eID="gen39275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">such things as ye have--</hi>literally, "present things" (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.11">Php 4:11</reference>).<div eID="gen39276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee--</hi>A promise tantamount to this was given to Jacob (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.15">Ge 28:15</reference>), to Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.31.6">De 31:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.31.8">8</reference>), to Joshua (<reference osisRef="Josh.1.5">Jos 1:5</reference>), to Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.28.20">1Ch 28:20</reference>). It is therefore like a divine adage. What was said to them, extends also to us. He will neither withdraw His presence ("never leave thee") nor His help ("nor forsake thee") [Bengel]. <div eID="gen39277" type="x-p"/>
entries.a2511b5939df49c77931e6ee1dfefe8a4802bfc5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18601"/><div sID="gen39278" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18601"/><hi type="bold">6. may--</hi>rather as Greek, expressing confidence actually realized, "So that we boldly (confidently) say" (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.4">Psa 56:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.56.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.6">118:6</reference>). Punctuate as both the Hebrew and the Greek require, "And (so) I will not fear: what (then) shall man do unto me?" <hi type="bold">7. Remember--</hi>so as to imitate: not to invoke in prayer, as Rome teaches.<div eID="gen39278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39279" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have the rule--</hi>rather, "who have had the rule over you": your spiritual leaders.<div eID="gen39279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who--</hi>Greek, "the which": such persons as.<div eID="gen39280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39281" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have spoken unto you--</hi>"spake" (so the Greek aorist means) during their lifetime. This Epistle was among those written later, when many of the heads of the Jerusalem Church had passed away.<div eID="gen39281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39282" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whose faith--</hi>even unto death: probably death by martyrdom, as in the case of the instances of faith in <reference osisRef="Heb.11.35">He 11:35</reference>. Stephen, James the brother of our Lord and bishop of Jerusalem, as well as James the brother of John (<reference osisRef="Acts.12.2">Ac 12:2</reference>), in the Palestinian Church, which Paul addresses, suffered martyrdom.<div eID="gen39282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">considering--</hi>Greek, "looking up to," "diligently contemplating all over," as an artist would a model.<div eID="gen39283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39284" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the end--</hi>the termination, at death. The Greek, is used of decease (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.31">Lu 9:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.15">2Pe 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen39284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39285" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of their conversation--</hi>"manner of life": "religious walk" (<reference osisRef="Gal.1.13">Ga 1:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.22">Ep 4:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.3.13">Jas 3:13</reference>). Considering how they manifested the soundness of their faith by their holy walk, which they maintained even to the end of that walk (their death by martyrdom). <div eID="gen39285" type="x-p"/>
entries.50160a0926dad20364446d65f4a5d260d77f7c3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18597"/><div sID="gen39264" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18597"/>7. Two manifestations of "brotherly love," hospitality and care for those in bonds.<div eID="gen39264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39265" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Be not forgetful--</hi>implying it was a duty which they all recognized, but which they might forget to act on (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.3">He 13:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.7.16">7, 16</reference>). The enemies of Christianity themselves have noticed the practice of this virtue among Christians [Julian, Epistles, 49].<div eID="gen39265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39266" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">entertained angels unawares--</hi>Abraham and Lot did so (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.2">Ge 18:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.19.1">19:1</reference>). To obviate the natural distrust felt of strangers, Paul says, an unknown guest may be better than he looks: he may be unexpectedly found to be as much a messenger of God for good, as the angels (whose name means messenger) are; nay more, if a Christian, he represents Christ Himself. There is a play on the same Greek word, Be not forgetful and unaware; let not the duty of hospitality to strangers escape you; for, by entertaining strangers, it has escaped the entertainers that they were entertaining angels. Not unconscious and forgetful of the duty, they have unconsciously brought on themselves the blessing. <div eID="gen39266" type="x-p"/>
entries.80e58130912584fe307bd85e7ecd66eec6c9a842: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18602"/><div sID="gen39286" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18602"/>8. This verse is not, as some read it, in apposition with "the end of their conversation" (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.7">He 13:7</reference>), but forms the transition. "Jesus Christ, yesterday and to-day (is) the same, and (shall be the same) unto the ages (that is, unto all ages)." The Jesus Christ (the full name being given, to mark with affectionate solemnity both His person and His office) who supported your spiritual rulers through life even unto their end "yesterday" (in times past), being at once "the Author and the Finisher of their faith" (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">He 12:2</reference>), remains still the same Jesus Christ "to-day," ready to help you also, if like them you walk by "faith" in Him. Compare "this same Jesus," <reference osisRef="Acts.1.11">Ac 1:11</reference>. He who yesterday (proverbial for the past time) suffered and died, is to-day in glory (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.18">Re 1:18</reference>). "As night comes between yesterday and to-day, and yet night itself is swallowed up by yesterday and to-day, so the "suffering" did not so interrupt the glory of Jesus Christ which was of yesterday, and that which is to-day, as not to continue to be the same. He is the same yesterday, before He came into the world, and to-day, in heaven. Yesterday in the time of our predecessors, and to-day in our age" [Bengel]. So the doctrine is the same, not variable: this verse thus forms the transition between <reference osisRef="Heb.13.7">He 13:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Heb.13.9">He 13:9</reference>. He is always "the same" (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.12">He 1:12</reference>). The same in the Old and in the New Testament. <div eID="gen39286" type="x-p"/>
entries.19f8a5af547d41370e9100ce1adfb3ff994dead5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18603"/><div sID="gen39287" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18603"/><hi type="bold">9. about--</hi>rather, as oldest manuscripts read, "carried aside"; namely, compare <reference osisRef="Eph.4.14">Ep 4:14</reference>.<div eID="gen39287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39288" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">divers--</hi>differing from the one faith in the one and the same Jesus Christ, as taught by them who had the rule over you (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.7">He 13:7</reference>).<div eID="gen39288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39289" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">strange--</hi>foreign to the truth.<div eID="gen39289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39290" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doctrines--</hi>"teachings."<div eID="gen39290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39291" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">established with grace; not with meats--</hi>not with observances of Jewish distinctions between clean and unclean meats, to which ascetic Judaizers added in Christian times the rejection of some meats, and the use of others: noticed also by Paul in <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.8">1Co 8:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.13">13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.13">6:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">Ro 14:17</reference>, an exact parallel to this verse: these are some of the "divers and strange doctrines" of the previous sentence. Christ's body offered once for all for us, is our true spiritual "meat" to "eat" (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.10">He 13:10</reference>), "the stay and the staff of bread" (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Is 3:1</reference>), the mean of all "grace."<div eID="gen39291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39292" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which have not profited--</hi>Greek, "in which they who walked were not profited"; namely, in respect to justification, perfect cleansing of the conscience, and sanctification. Compare on "walked," <reference osisRef="Acts.21.21">Ac 21:21</reference>; namely, with superstitious scrupulosity, as though the worship of God in itself consisted in such legal observances. <div eID="gen39292" type="x-p"/>
entries.1be7395c2764fd69b3c61eb204e2924398e0ca80: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18604"/><div sID="gen39293" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18604"/>10. Christianity and Judaism are so totally distinct, that "they who serve the (Jewish) tabernacle," have no right to eat our spiritual Gospel meat, namely, the Jewish priests, and those who follow their guidance in serving the ceremonial ordinance. He says, "serve the tabernacle," not "serve IN the tabernacle." Contrast with this servile worship ours.<div eID="gen39293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39294" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">an altar--</hi>the cross of Christ, whereon His body was offered. The Lord's table represents this altar, the cross; as the bread and wine represent the sacrifice offered on it. Our meat, which we by faith spiritually eat, is the flesh of Christ, in contrast to the typical ceremonial meats. The two cannot be combined (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.2">Ga 5:2</reference>). That not a literal eating of the sacrifice of Christ is meant in the Lord's Supper, but a spiritual is meant, appears from comparing <reference osisRef="Heb.13.9">He 13:9</reference> with <reference osisRef="Heb.13.10">He 13:10</reference>, "with GRACE, NOT with MEATS." <div eID="gen39294" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b3d06fd51d94e8f48185878fb54129bab786bf1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18605"/><div sID="gen39295" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18605"/>11-12. For just as "the bodies of those beasts whose blood is brought into the sanctuary by ... are burned without the camp," so "Jesus also that ... suffered without the gate" of ceremonial Judaism, of which His crucifixion outside the gate of Jerusalem is a type.<div eID="gen39295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39296" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>reason why they who serve the tabernacle, are excluded from share in Christ; because His sacrifice is not like one of those sacrifices in which they had a share but answers to one which was "wholly burned" outside (the Greek is "burnt completely," "consumed by burning"), and which consequently they could not eat of. <reference osisRef="Lev.6.30">Le 6:30</reference>, gives the general rule, "No sin offering whereof any of the blood is brought into the tabernacle of the congregation to reconcile withal in the holy place, shall be eaten; it shall be burnt in the fire." The sin offerings are twofold: the outward, whose blood was sprinkled on the outward altar, and of whose bodies the priests might eat; and the inward, the reverse.<div eID="gen39296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39297" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sanctuary--</hi>here the Holy of Holies, into which the blood of the sin offering was brought on the day of atonement.<div eID="gen39297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without the camp--</hi>in which were the tabernacle and Levitical priests and legal worshippers, during Israel's journey through the wilderness; replaced afterwards by Jerusalem (containing the temple), outside of whose walls Jesus was crucified. <div eID="gen39298" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb7ed2224e572deabc24dca012c96905fe424ff8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18607"/><div sID="gen39303" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18607"/><hi type="bold">13. therefore--</hi>This "therefore" breathes the deliberate fortitude of believers [Bengel].<div eID="gen39303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39304" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without the camp--</hi>"outside the legal polity" [Theodoret] of Judaism (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.13.11">He 13:11</reference>) "Faith considers Jerusalem itself as a camp, not a city" [Bengel]. He contrasts with the Jews, who serve an earthly sanctuary, the Christians to whom the altar in heaven stands open, while it is closed against the Jews. As Jesus suffered without the gate, so spiritually must those who desire to belong to Him, withdraw from the earthly Jerusalem and its sanctuary, as from this world in general. There is a reference to <reference osisRef="Exod.33.7">Ex 33:7</reference>, when the tabernacle was moved without the camp, which had become polluted by the people's idolatry of the golden calves; so that "every one who sought the Lord went out unto the tabernacle of the congregation (as Moses called the tabernacle outside the camp), which was without the camp"; a lively type of what the Hebrews should do, namely, come out of the carnal worship of the earthly Jerusalem to worship God in Christ in spirit, and of what we all ought to do, namely, come out from all carnalism, worldly formalism, and mere sensuous worship, and know Jesus in His spiritual power apart from worldliness, seeing that "we have no continuing city" (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.14">He 13:14</reference>).<div eID="gen39304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39305" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bearing--</hi>as Simon of Cyrene did.<div eID="gen39305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his reproach--</hi>the reproach which He bare, and which all His people bear with Him. <div eID="gen39306" type="x-p"/>
entries.3c765aaa6544fe1dd50b0ed6fa6c58e265cd1ecf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18608"/><div sID="gen39307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18608"/><hi type="bold">14. here--</hi>on earth. Those Hebrews who clung to the earthly sanctuary are representatives of all who cling to this earth. The earthly Jerusalem proved to be no "abiding city," having been destroyed shortly after this Epistle was written, and with it fell the Jewish civil and religious polity; a type of the whole of our present earthly order of things soon to perish.<div eID="gen39307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one to come--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.2.5">He 2:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.10">11:10</reference>, 14, 16; 12:22; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.20">Php 3:20</reference>). <div eID="gen39308" type="x-p"/>
entries.079286fadb9d2941b9e08283b8994dc38a47156a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18609"/><div sID="gen39309" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18609"/>15. As the "altar" was mentioned in <reference osisRef="Heb.13.10">He 13:10</reference>, so the "sacrifices" here (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pe 2:5</reference>, namely, praise and doing good, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.16">He 13:16</reference>). Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.119.108">Psa 119:108</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Ro 12:1</reference>.<div eID="gen39309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39310" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">By him--</hi>as the Mediator of our prayers and praises (<reference osisRef="John.14.13">Joh 14:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.14">14</reference>); not by Jewish observances (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.14">Psa 50:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.69.30">69:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.69.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.107.22">107:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.17">116:17</reference>). It was an old saying of the rabbis, "At a future time all sacrifices shall cease, but praises shall not cease."<div eID="gen39310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39311" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of praise--</hi>for salvation.<div eID="gen39311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39312" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">continually--</hi>not merely at fixed seasons, as those on which the legal sacrifices were offered, but throughout all our lives.<div eID="gen39312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fruit of our lips--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Is 57:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.14.2">Ho 14:2</reference>).<div eID="gen39313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39314" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">giving thanks--</hi>Greek, "confessing." Bengel remarks that the Hebrew, "todah," is beautifully emphatic. It literally means "acknowledgment" or "confession." In praising a creature, we may easily exceed the truth; but in praising God we have only to go on confessing what He really is to us. Hence it is impossible to exceed the truth, and here is genuine praise. <div eID="gen39314" type="x-p"/>
entries.1a70e095b303316b175cf0909515e0f4c7bfbdb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18610"/><div sID="gen39315" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18610"/><hi type="bold">16. But--</hi>But the sacrifice of praise with the lips (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">He 13:15</reference>) is not enough; there must be also doing good (beneficence) and communicating (that is, imparting a share of your means, <reference osisRef="Gal.6.6">Ga 6:6</reference>) to the needy.<div eID="gen39315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with such--</hi>and not mere ritualistic sacrifices. <div eID="gen39316" type="x-p"/>
entries.dbe77c9aa6ddc3fd67466cc1debb958e058b142d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18611"/><div sID="gen39317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18611"/><hi type="bold">17. Obey them that have the rule over you--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Heb.13.7">He 13:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.24">24</reference>). This threefold mention of the rulers is peculiar to this Epistle. In other Epistles Paul includes the rulers in his exhortations. But here the address is limited to the general body of the Church, in contrast to the rulers to whom they are charged to yield reverent submission. Now this is just what might be expected when the apostle of the Gentiles was writing to the Palestine Christians, among whom James and the eleven apostles had exercised a more immediate authority. It was important he should not seem to set himself in opposition to their guides, but rather strengthen their hands; he claims no authority directly or indirectly over these rulers themselves [Birks]. "Remember" your deceased rulers (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.7">He 13:7</reference>). "Obey" your living rulers; nay, more, not only obey in cases where no sacrifice of self is required, and where you are persuaded they are right (so the Greek, for "obey"), but "submit yourselves" as a matter of dutiful yielding, when your judgment and natural will incline you in an opposite direction.<div eID="gen39317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they--</hi>on their part; so the Greek. As they do their part, so do you yours. So Paul exhorts, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12">1Th 5:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.13">13</reference>.<div eID="gen39318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watch--</hi>"are vigilant" (Greek).<div eID="gen39319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for--</hi>Greek, "in behalf of."<div eID="gen39320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39321" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">must give account--</hi>The strongest stimulus to watchfulness (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.34-Mark.13.37">Mr 13:34-37</reference>). Chrysostom was deeply struck with these words, as he tells us [On the Priesthood, 6], "The fear of this threat continually agitates my soul."<div eID="gen39321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39322" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do it--</hi>"watch for your soul's eternal salvation." It is a perilous responsibility for a man to have to give account for others' deeds, who is not sufficient for his own [Estius, from Aquinas]. I wonder whether it be possible that any of the rulers should be saved [Chrysostom]. Compare Paul's address to the elders, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.1-1Cor.4.5">1Co 4:1-5</reference>, where also he connects ministers' responsibility with the account to be hereafter given (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.4">1Pe 5:4</reference>).<div eID="gen39322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with joy--</hi>at your obedience; anticipating, too, that you shall be their "joy" in the day of giving account (<reference osisRef="Phil.4.1">Php 4:1</reference>).<div eID="gen39323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not with grief--</hi>at your disobedience; apprehending also that in the day of account you may be among the lost, instead of being their crown of rejoicing. In giving account, the stewards are liable to blame if aught be lost to the Master. "Mitigate their toil by every office of attention and respect, that with alacrity, rather than with grief, they may fulfil their duty, arduous enough in itself, even though no unpleasantness be added on your part" [Grotius].<div eID="gen39324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39325" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that--</hi>Grief in your pastors is unprofitable for you, for it weakens their spiritual power; nay, more, "the groans (so the Greek for 'grief') of other creatures are heard; how much more of pastors!" [Bengel]. So God will be provoked to avenge on you their "groaning" (Greek). If they must render God an account of their negligence, so must you for your ingratitude to them [Grotius]. <div eID="gen39325" type="x-p"/>
entries.2b704d93852be46d2d9d49b2b695c5d2b3033ede: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18612"/><div sID="gen39326" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18612"/><hi type="bold">18. Pray for us--</hi>Paul usually requests the Church's intercessions for him in closing his Epistles, just as he begins with assuring them of his having them at heart in his prayers (but in this Epistle not till <reference osisRef="Heb.13.20">He 13:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.21">21</reference>), <reference osisRef="Rom.15.30">Ro 15:30</reference>. "Us," includes both himself and his companions; he passes to himself alone, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.19">He 13:19</reference>.<div eID="gen39326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39327" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we trust we have a good conscience--</hi>in spite of your former jealousies, and the charges of my Jewish enemies at Jerusalem, which have been the occasion of my imprisonment at Rome. In refutation of the Jews' aspersions, he asserts in the same language as here his own conscientiousness before God and man, <reference osisRef="Acts.23.1-Acts.3.24">Ac 23:1-3; 24</reference>:16, 20, 21 (wherein he virtually implies that his reply to Ananias was not sinful impatience; for, indeed, it was a prophecy which he was inspired at the moment to utter, and which was fulfilled soon after).<div eID="gen39327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we trust--</hi>Greek, "we are persuaded," in the oldest manuscripts. Good conscience produces confidence, where the Holy Spirit rules the conscience (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.1">Ro 9:1</reference>).<div eID="gen39328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39329" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">honestly--</hi>"in a good way." The same Greek word as "good conscience." Literally, "rightly," "becomingly." <div eID="gen39329" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b42a8e20584619f338cb4f0a9b9449ae0687675: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18613"/><div sID="gen39330" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18613"/><hi type="bold">19. the rather--</hi>Greek, "I the more abundantly beseech you."<div eID="gen39330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39331" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to do this--</hi>to pray for me.<div eID="gen39331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39332" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that I may be restored to you--</hi>(Phm 22). It is here first in the letter he mentions himself, in a way so unobtrusive, as not to prejudice his Hebrew readers against him, which would have been the result had he commenced this as his other Epistles, with authoritatively announcing his name and apostolic commission. <div eID="gen39332" type="x-p"/>
entries.77cb087ea7f3e1f81969a31468f89830c8f54b0d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18614"/><div sID="gen39333" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18614"/>20. Concluding prayer.<div eID="gen39333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God of peace--</hi>So Paul, <reference osisRef="Rom.15.33">Ro 15:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.16.20">16:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.11">2Co 13:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.9">Php 4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.23">1Th 5:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.16">2Th 3:16</reference>. The Judaizing of the Hebrews was calculated to sow seeds of discord among them, of disobedience to their pastors (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">He 13:17</reference>), and of alienation towards Paul. The God of peace by giving unity of true doctrine, will unite them in mutual love.<div eID="gen39334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39335" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">brought again from the dead--</hi>Greek, "brought up," &c.: God brought the Shepherd; the Shepherd shall bring the flock. Here only in the Epistle he mentions the resurrection. He would not conclude without mentioning 'the connecting link between the two truths mainly discussed; the one perfect sacrifice and the continual priestly intercession--the depth of His humiliation and the height of His glory--the "altar" of the cross and the ascension to the heavenly Holy of Holies.<div eID="gen39335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Lord Jesus--</hi>the title marking His person and His Lordship over us. But <reference osisRef="Heb.13.21">He 13:21</reference>, "through Jesus Christ." His office, as the Anointed of the Spirit, making Him the medium of communicating the Spirit to us, the holy unction flowing down from the Head on the members (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.36">Ac 2:36</reference>).<div eID="gen39336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39337" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">great--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.4.14">He 4:14</reference>).<div eID="gen39337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39338" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shepherd of the sheep--</hi>A title familiar to his Hebrew readers, from their Old Testament (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.11">Is 63:11</reference>; Septuagint): primarily Moses, antitypically Christ: already compared together, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.2-Heb.3.7">He 3:2-7</reference>. The transition is natural from their earthly pastors (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">He 13:17</reference>), to the Chief Pastor, as in <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.1-1Pet.5.4">1Pe 5:1-4</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference> and Jesus' own words, <reference osisRef="John.10.2">Joh 10:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.11.14">11, 14</reference>.<div eID="gen39338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through the blood--</hi>Greek, "in," in virtue of the blood (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.9">He 2:9</reference>); it was because of His bloody death for us, that the Father raised and crowned Him with glory. The "blood" was the seal of the everlasting covenant entered into between the Father and Son; in virtue of the Son's blood, first Christ was raised, then Christ's people shall be so (<reference osisRef="Zech.9.11">Zec 9:11</reference>, seemingly referred to here; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>).<div eID="gen39339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39340" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting--</hi>The everlastingness of the covenant necessitated the resurrection. This clause, "the blood of the everlasting covenant," is a summary retrospect of the Epistle (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.9.12">He 9:12</reference>). <div eID="gen39340" type="x-p"/>
entries.febb2344fe0bc99769cbdfabbacc5e97511aa6a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18615"/><div sID="gen39341" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18615"/><hi type="bold">21. Make you perfect--</hi>properly said of healing a rent; join you together in perfect harmony [Bengel].<div eID="gen39341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39342" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to do his will, working in you--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Heb.10.36">He 10:36</reference>); rather as Greek, "doing in you." Whatever good we do, God does in us.<div eID="gen39342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39343" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">well-pleasing in his sight--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Is 53:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.10">Ep 5:10</reference>).<div eID="gen39343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39344" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">through Jesus Christ--</hi>"God doing (working) in you that ... through Jesus Christ" (<reference osisRef="Phil.1.11">Php 1:11</reference>).<div eID="gen39344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39345" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to whom--</hi>to Christ. He closes as he began (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.1-Heb.1.14">He 1:1-14</reference>), with giving glory to Christ. <div eID="gen39345" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1e404e5af04723836d4ba7dc05b995f3b36f254: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18616"/><div sID="gen39346" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18616"/><hi type="bold">22. suffer the word--</hi>The Hebrews not being the section of the Church assigned to Paul (but the Gentiles), he uses gentle entreaty, rather than authoritative command.<div eID="gen39346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39347" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">few words--</hi>compared with what might be said on so important a subject. Few, in an Epistle which is more of a treatise than an Epistle (compare <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.12">1Pe 5:12</reference>). On the seeming inconsistency with <reference osisRef="Gal.6.11">Ga 6:11</reference>, compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Gal.6.11">Ga 6:11</reference>. <div eID="gen39347" type="x-p"/>
entries.f03205775199f98d316be8d77c256503ab61f46f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18617"/><div sID="gen39348" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18617"/><hi type="bold">23. our brother Timothy--</hi>So Paul, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.17">1Co 4:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1">2Co 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.1">Col 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.2">1Th 3:2</reference>.<div eID="gen39348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39349" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is set at liberty--</hi>from prison. So Aristarchus was imprisoned with Paul. Birks translates, "dismissed," "sent away," namely, on a mission to Greece, as Paul promised (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.19">Php 2:19</reference>). However, some kind of previous detention is implied before his being let go to Philippi. Paul, though now at large, was still in Italy, whence he sends the salutations of Italian Christians (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.24">He 13:24</reference>), waiting for Timothy to join him, so as to start for Jerusalem: we know from <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>, he and Timothy were together at Ephesus after his departing from Italy eastward. He probably left Timothy there and went to Philippi as he had promised. Paul implies that if Timothy shall not come shortly, he will start on his journey to the Hebrews at once. <div eID="gen39349" type="x-p"/>
entries.997fba639a7ef74a7e69afff8886e20936d2735e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18618"/><div sID="gen39350" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18618"/><hi type="bold">24. all--</hi>The Scriptures are intended for all, young and old, not merely for ministers. Compare the different classes addressed, "wives," <reference osisRef="Eph.5.22">Ep 5:22</reference>; little children, <reference osisRef="1John.2.18">1Jo 2:18</reference>; "all," <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.8">1Pe 3:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.5">5:5</reference>. He says here "all," for the Hebrews whom he addresses were not all in one place, though the Jerusalem Hebrews are chiefly addressed.<div eID="gen39350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39351" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">They of Italy--</hi>not merely the brethren at Rome, but of other places in Italy. <div eID="gen39351" type="x-p"/>
entries.cff1449fd6386bd1e0dd141a10b01376759158f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18619"/><div sID="gen39352" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18619"/>25. Paul's characteristic salutation in every one of his other thirteen Epistles, as he says himself, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.21">1Co 16:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.16.23">23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.18">Col 4:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.3.17">2Th 3:17</reference>. It is found in no Epistle written by any other apostle in Paul's lifetime. It is used in <reference osisRef="Rev.22.21">Re 22:21</reference>, written subsequently, and in Clement of Rome. Being known to be his badge, it is not used by others in his lifetime. The Greek here is, "The grace (namely, of our Lord Jesus Christ) be with you all." <chapter eID="Heb.13"/><div eID="gen39352" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen38143" osisID="Heb" type="book"/>

entries.221f3593fcb584e3b841df03bc9422ada60419f0: <div eID="gen53831" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen53832" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen53833" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen53833" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen53832" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen53834" type="x-p"/> Exhortations to hospitality to Strangers, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.1">Heb 13:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.2">Heb 13:2</reference>. Kindness to those in bonds, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.3">Heb 13:3</reference>. Concerning marriage, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.4">Heb 13:4</reference>. Against covetousness, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.5">Heb 13:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.6">Heb 13:6</reference>. How they should imitate their teachers, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.7">Heb 13:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.8">Heb 13:8</reference>. To avoid strange doctrines, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.9">Heb 13:9</reference>. Of the Jewish sin-offerings, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.10">Heb 13:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.11">Heb 13:11</reference>. Jesus suffered without the gate, and we should openly confess him and bear his reproach, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.12">Heb 13:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.13">Heb 13:13</reference>. Here we have no permanent residence; and while we live should devote ourselves to God, and live to do good, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.14-Heb.13.16">Heb 13:14-16</reference>. We should obey them that have the rule over us, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.17">Heb 13:17</reference>. The apostle exhorts them to pray for him, that he might be restored to them the sooner, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.18">Heb 13:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.19">Heb 13:19</reference>. Commends them to God in a very solemn prayer, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.20">Heb 13:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.21">Heb 13:21</reference>. Entreats them to bear the word of exhortation, mentions Timothy, and concludes with the apostolical benediction, <reference osisRef="Heb.13.22-Heb.13.25">Heb 13:22-25</reference>. <div eID="gen53834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53835" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen53835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53836" type="x-p"/> Let brotherly love continue - Be all of one heart and one soul. <div eID="gen53836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53837" type="x-p"/> Feel for, comfort, and support each other; and remember that he who professes to love God should love his brother also. They had this brotherly love among them; they should take care to retain it. As God is remarkable for his φιλανθρωπια, philanthropy, or love to man, so should they be for φιλαδελφια, or love to each other. See the note on <reference osisRef="Tit.3.4">Tit 3:4</reference>.
entries.2e6f550b159b4daee896af8987365aa32900cab4: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen53837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53838" type="x-p"/> To entertain stranger's - In those early times, when there were scarcely any public inns or houses of entertainment, it was an office of charity and mercy to receive, lodge, and entertain travelers; and this is what the apostle particularly recommends. <div eID="gen53838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen53839" type="x-p"/> Entertained angels - Abraham and Lot are the persons particularly referred to. Their history, the angels whom they entertained, not knowing them to be such, and the good they derived from exercising their hospitality on these occasions, are well known; and have been particularly referred to in the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.18.3">Gen 18:3</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Gen.19.2">Gen 19:2</reference> (note).
