So <hi type="italic">Stuart </hi>and <hi type="italic">Bloomfield. </hi>The first renders the verse thus, —<div eID="gen134257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134258" type="x-p"/>“Besides, he doth not at all help the angels, but he helpeth the seed of Abraham.”<div eID="gen134258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134259" type="x-p"/>The present, the historical present, is used for the past; or if we render οὐ γὰρ δήπου “for nowhere,” the reference is to Scripture; nowhere in Scripture is such a thing recorded.<div eID="gen134259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134260" type="x-p"/>But to “take hold on” is sufficiently plain and very expressive. Christ took hold on Peter when he was sinking, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.14.31">Matthew 14:31</reference>:) it is the same verb. Our Savior took not hold on the angels when sinking into ruin, but he did take hold on the seed of Abraham to save them from perdition. The connection seems to be with the preceding verses; therefore γὰρ ought to be rendered “for” and not “besides,” as by <hi type="italic">Stuart, </hi>nor “moreover,” as by <hi type="italic">Macknight. </hi>A reason is given why Christ became partaker of flesh and blood; and the reason was, because he did not come to deliver angels but the seed of Abraham; that is, his spiritual, not his natural seed, for he speaks throughout of God’s sons and God’s children. See <reference osisRef="Bible:John.1.12 Bible:John.1.13">John 1:12, 13</reference>, where the born of God are represented to be those to whom Christ grants the privilege of children.<div eID="gen134260" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134255"/> <div sID="gen134261"/> <div sID="gen134262" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX L<div eID="gen134262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134263" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 3:4</hi> <hi type="italic"> He that built, etc.</hi> This verse has been considered as difficult with respect to the connection it has with the argument of the Apostle. <hi type="italic">Stuart </hi>states thus the difficulty, — “Moses as the <hi type="italic">delegate </hi>of God was the founder of the Jewish institution, and Christ is merely declared to be only a <hi type="italic">delegated founder, </hi>then in what way does the writer make out the superiority of Christ to Moses. Both were delegates of the same God, and both the founders of a new and divine dispensation. If Christ, then, is not here asserted to be founder in some other character than that of a <hi type="italic">delegate, </hi>I am unable to perceive any force in the writer’s argument.” Hence the Professor comes to the conclusion, that Christ is meant by the Apostle when he says, “He who built (or formed) all things is God,” conceiving that the argument is otherwise inconclusive.<div eID="gen134263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134264" type="x-p"/>Now, the mistake of the Professor is this, that he makes delegation to be the comparison and not the <hi type="italic">character </hi>of the delegation. That Christ’s power was delegated is quite evident from this passage: Christ is said to have been “appointed” in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.3.2">verse 2</reference>, and is said to be “faithful,” which implies that he had an office delegated to him. Then the delegation is undeniable; and what the Apostle evidently dwells upon is the superiority of the delegated power: Moses was faithful as a servant in God’s house; the people of Israel were previously Gods adopted people; but Christ has power, a delegated power, to make as it were a new people; he builds his own house. Moses was a part of the house in which he served; but as Christ builds his own house, he is worthy of more glory than Moses. These are the comparisons made by the Apostle.<div eID="gen134264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134265" type="x-p"/>Then this verse is introduced, and that for two reasons, — first, to shew that God built the house in which Moses served; and secondly, to intimate the divine power of Christ, as none but God builds all things. Moses’ house is called God’s house in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.3.2">verse 2</reference>; and Christ’s house is called his own in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.3.5">verse 5</reference>. Hence the obvious inference is, that he is one with God, as God only builds all things, though in his Mediatorial character he acts as God’s Apostle and high priest. The same kind of representation we find in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.1.2 Bible:Heb.1.10">the first chapter</reference>: it is said that by him God made the world; and afterwards that the Son is the Creator, who had founded the earth, and whose work are the heavens. Creative power, though exercised by Christ as a Mediator, must yet be a divine power.<div eID="gen134265" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134261"/> <div sID="gen134266"/> <div sID="gen134267" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX M<div eID="gen134267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134268" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 3:9.</hi> <hi type="italic">Tempted, etc.</hi> To understand this passage we must bear in mind the event referred to. The same year in which the people of Israel came forth from Egypt, they were distressed for water at Rephidim, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.17.1">Exodus 17:1</reference>;) and the place had two names given to it, Massah and Meribah, because the people tempted God and chided with Moses. The Lord did not swear <hi type="italic">then </hi>that they should not enter into the land of Canaan; but this was on the following year, after the return of the spies. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Num.14.20-Num.14.38">Numbers 14:20-38</reference>.) And God said then that they had tempted him “ten times;” that is, during the short time since their deliverance from Egypt. It was after <hi type="italic">ten </hi>temptations that God deprived them of the promised land.<div eID="gen134268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134269" type="x-p"/>Bearing in mind these facts, we shall be able to see the full force of the passage. The “provocation” or contention, and “temptation” refer clearly to the latter instance, as recorded in <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.14">Numbers 14</reference>, because it was then that God swear that the people should not enter into his rest. The people’s conduct was alike in both instances.<div eID="gen134269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134270" type="x-p"/>To connect “forty years” with “grieved” was the work of the Punctuists, and this mistake the Apostle corrected; and it is to be observed that he did not follow in this instance the <hi type="italic">Septuagint, </hi>in which the words are arranged as divided by the Masorites. Such a rendering as would correspond with the Hebrew is as follows, — “Today when ye hear his voice,<div eID="gen134270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134271" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> Harden not your hearts as in the provocation, In the day of temptation in the wilderness.<div eID="gen134271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134272" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi> When your fathers tempted me, they proved me And saw my works forty years:<div eID="gen134272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134273" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10</hi> I was therefore offended with that generation and said, Always do they go astray in heart, And they have not known my ways;<div eID="gen134273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134274" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> So that I swear in my wrath, They shall by no means enter into my rest.’”<div eID="gen134274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134275" type="x-p"/>The meaning of the ninth verse is, that when the children of Israel tempted God, they proved him, <hi type="italic">i.e., </hi>found out by bitter experience how great his displeasure was, and saw his works or his dealings with them for forty years. He retained them in the wilderness during that period until the death of all who disbelieved his word at the return of the spies; he gave them this proof of his displeasure. “Therefore” in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.3.11">verse 11</reference> is connected with “tempted;” it was because they tempted him that he was offended with them so as to swear that they should not enter into his rest. There is evidently a <foreign xml:lang="he">ו</foreign> left out in Hebrew, found only in one MS.; but it is required by the future form of the verb. To “go astray in heart” was to disbelieve God’s word, (see <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.3.12">verse 12</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.14.11">Numbers 14:11</reference>;) and not to have known Gods ways, was not to recognize his power, and goodness, and faithfulness in their deliverance from Egypt. See <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.14.22">Numbers 14:22</reference>. Not to know here does not mean what <hi type="italic">Stuart </hi>says, not to approve, but not to comprehend or understand God’s ways, or not to recognize them as his ways or doings.<div eID="gen134275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134276" type="x-p"/>The last line is in the form of an oath, “If they shall enter,” etc.; but when in this defective form, the “if” may be rendered as a strong negative, “by no means.” <hi type="italic">Doddridge </hi>has “never,” and <hi type="italic">Macknight</hi> “not,” in which he has been followed by <hi type="italic">Stuart.</hi><div eID="gen134276" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134266"/> <div sID="gen134277"/> <div sID="gen134278" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX N<div eID="gen134278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134279" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 3:15</hi> <hi type="italic">While it is said, etc.</hi> No doubt the connection first referred to in the note is the most suitable. This verse is as it were the heading of what follows; but to put the sixteenth verse in an interrogatory form, as is done by <hi type="italic">Stuart, </hi>seems not suitable to the passage. I would render the words thus, —<div eID="gen134279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15. </hi>With regard to what is said, “Today, when ye hear his<div eID="gen134280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134281" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16. </hi>voice, harden not your hearts as in the provocation,” some indeed when they heard did provoke, but not all who came<div eID="gen134281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134282" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi> out of Egypt under Moses: but with whom was he offended for forty years? was it not with those who sinned, whose<div eID="gen134282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134283" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18. </hi>carcasses fell in the wilderness? And to whom did he swear that they should not enter into his rest, but to those who did not believe?<div eID="gen134283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134284" type="x-p"/>The “provocation” is the subject; who offered it are then mentioned; and afterwards the cause of it, the want of faith.<div eID="gen134284" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134277"/> <div sID="gen134285"/> <div sID="gen134286" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX O<div eID="gen134286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 4:2</hi> <hi type="italic"> For unto us</hi> <hi type="italic">was the Gospel preached, etc.</hi> Literally it is, “For we have been evangelized.” <hi type="italic">Doddridge </hi>has, “For we are made partakers of the good tidings;” <hi type="italic">Macknight,</hi> “For we also have received the good tidings;” and <hi type="italic">Stuart,</hi> “For to us also blessings are proclaimed.” Perhaps the most literal version would be, “For we also have had good tidings.” The same form of words occurs again in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.4.6">verse 6</reference>, “And they to whom it was first preached,” etc.; rather, “And they who had first good tidings,” etc. The good tidings were evidently the promise of rest.<div eID="gen134287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134288" type="x-p"/>“The word preached” is literally “the word of hearing;” that is, the word heard, a noun being put for a participle, a common thing in Hebrew.<div eID="gen134288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134289" type="x-p"/>Though there are several MSS. and the Greek fathers in favor of “mixed” being in the accusative case, agreeing with “them,” “who united not by faith with those who heard,” <hi type="italic">i.e., </hi>obeyed; yet the <hi type="italic">Vulgate </hi>and the <hi type="italic">Syriac </hi>countenance our present reading, which has been adopted by <hi type="italic">Erasmus, Beza, </hi>Dr. <hi type="italic">Owen, </hi>and most modern divines, as being most suitable to the passage.<div eID="gen134289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134290" type="x-p"/>Our version is followed by <hi type="italic">Doddridge </hi>and <hi type="italic">Macknight. </hi>The version of <hi type="italic">Stuart </hi>is the same with that of <hi type="italic">Calvin,</hi> “being not connected with faith in those who heard it.” The <hi type="italic">Syriac </hi>seems the most literal, “being not mingled with faith by them who heard it.” They had not the ingredient of faith to mix up as it were with it. Instead of receiving the promise, they refused and rejected it, as though it were an unwholesome and disagreeable draught. The word is used in <reference osisRef="Bible:2Macc.15.39">2 Macc. 15:39</reference>, of wine <hi type="italic">mingled </hi>with water.<div eID="gen134290" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134285"/> <div sID="gen134291"/> <div sID="gen134292" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX P<div eID="gen134292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134293" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 4:12.</hi> <hi type="italic">For the word of God, etc</hi>. Some, as <hi type="italic">Stuart </hi>and <hi type="italic">Bloomfield, </hi>view “the word” here as minatory, being a threatening to the unbelievers before mentioned. Though it may be so viewed, yet it seems not to be right to translate λόγος; “threatening,” as done by <hi type="italic">Stuart.</hi><div eID="gen134293" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134291"/> <div sID="gen134294"/> <div sID="gen134295" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX Q<div eID="gen134295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134296" type="x-p"/>“Quick” or living, and “powerful” or efficacious, are regarded by many as meaning nearly the same thing; but “living” designates what is valid, what continues in force, as opposed to what is dead and no longer existing; and “efficacious” refers to the effect, capable of producing the effect designed. Exclusion from rest as to unbelievers was still living, still in force, abiding the same without any change. See <reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.23 Bible:1Pet.1.25">1 Peter 1:23, 25</reference>. It was also in full power so as effectually to exclude from rest all who did not believe. And then to prevent every evasion, so that no one might think a mere profession sufficient, or rather to guard against the incipient seduction of sin, he compares this “word” to a sword which can dissect the whole well­compacted frame of man, so that even the very marrow may be discovered; and then passing from this simile, he says that this “word” is capable of judging the thoughts and purposes of the heart. And in order to identify as it were this “word” with God himself; he immediately refers to God’s omniscience. The design of the Apostle seems to have been to guard the Hebrews against the deceitfulness of sin; so that they might not give heed to any of its hidden suggestions.<div eID="gen134296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134297" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Stuart </hi>makes the transition from the “word” to God at the end of the twelfth verse, and renders the clause thus, “He also judgeth the thoughts and purposes of the heart.” But this clause may more properly be viewed as explanatory of what is said of the two-edged sword.<div eID="gen134297" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134294"/> <div sID="gen134298"/> <div sID="gen134299" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX R<div eID="gen134299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 4:12.</hi> <hi type="italic">Two­edged sword, etc</hi> Whether the penetrating, or convincing, or killing power of the “word” is set forth by the metaphor of the “sword,” has been controverted. <hi type="italic">Beza </hi>and <hi type="italic">Scott, </hi>as well as <hi type="italic">Calvin, </hi>regard its convincing <hi type="italic">and </hi>killing power as intended. “It enters,” says <hi type="italic">Beta,</hi> “into the inmost recesses of the soul, so that it indicts on the perverse a deadly wound, and by killing the old man quickens into life the elect.” <hi type="italic">Stuart </hi>views its killing power as alone intended: “The sense is,” he observes, “that the divine commination is of <hi type="italic">most deadly </hi>punitive efficacy.”<div eID="gen134300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134301" type="x-p"/>Now, if the whole passage be duly considered in connection with what is gone before, there will appear a sufficient reason to conclude, that the metaphor of “the sword “is only intended to shew that the “word” reaches to all the inward workings of the soul, that it extends to the motives and the most hidden thoughts and purposes of the heart. The last clause in the 12th verse clearly explains what is meant by the “sword;” and this is further confirmed by the following verse, where it is said that all things are naked and open to God, of whose word he speaks, and with whom we have to do. All this seems to concur with the purpose for which the words were introduced, that is, to warn the Hebrews of the danger of listening to the seductive and deceiving power of sin.<div eID="gen134301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134302" type="x-p"/>As to the 13th verse, <hi type="italic">Bloomfield </hi>suggests a transposition which would render the transition from God’s word to God himself much more easy, “Moreover there exists no creature that is not manifest in the sight of him with whom we have to do; but all things are naked and exposed to his eyes.” But the construction here is similar to what we have noticed in two previous instances, <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.2.9 Bible:Heb.2.17 Bible:Heb.2.18">chapter 2:9, and 17, 18</reference>; the first and the last clause are connected, and the two middle clauses.<div eID="gen134302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134303" type="x-p"/>The last sentence is rendered by <hi type="italic">Grotius,</hi> “of whom is our word, <hi type="italic">i.e., </hi>of whom we speak; by <hi type="italic">Beza,</hi> “with whom we have to do; by <hi type="italic">Doddridge, Macknig</hi>h<hi type="italic">t, </hi>and <hi type="italic">Stuart,</hi> “to whom we must give an account.” Wherever λόγος signifies “account,” the verb “to render,” or a similar verb is connected with it. There are two instances in the <hi type="italic">Sept. </hi>where it stands alone with a pronoun in the dative case as here, and it means <hi type="italic">business, affair, </hi>or <hi type="italic">concern: </hi>see <reference osisRef="Bible:Judg.18.28">Judges 18:28</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.9.5">2 Kings 9:5</reference>. In the last passage it is connected also, as here, with the preposition πρὸς. There can therefore be no doubt but that our version is the right one, “with whom we have to do,” or literally, “with whom <hi type="italic">there is </hi>to us a concern.” There is no <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">usus loquendi</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">, </hi>as pleaded by some, in favor of the other meaning.<div eID="gen134303" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134298"/> <div sID="gen134304"/> <div sID="gen134305" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX S<div eID="gen134305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134306" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 6:1</hi> <hi type="italic">Therefore leaving, etc</hi> Authors differ as to the character of this passage, whether it be hortatory or didactic, that is, whether the Apostle, putting himself as it were with them, exhorts them to advance in knowledge, or, discharging the office of a teacher, he intimates the course which he means to pursue. <hi type="italic">Stuart </hi>and some others, as well as <hi type="italic">Calvin, </hi>take the first view, as though the Apostle had said, “As the perfect or grown up are alone capable of receiving strong food, it behooves us to quit the state of childhood and to advance into the state of manhood, so as to attain perfect knowledge.” It is said that this view comports better with what follows, “for it is impossible,” etc.<div eID="gen134306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134307" type="x-p"/>But there are especially two things in the passage which militate against this view, first, “not laying the foundation,” etc. which refers evidently to teaching; and secondly, the third verse, which also refers to teaching.<div eID="gen134307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134308" type="x-p"/>It is usual with the Apostle to speak of himself in the plural number: see, for instance, the 9th verse. “Therefore” is a general inference from what he had been saying, and not from a particular clause, as though he had said, “Such being the case with you, let me now therefore, in order to draw you onward, leave the first principles, and proceed to state things which are suitable to advanced Christians: it is not my purpose now to preach repentance and faith in which you have been already taught, and to do this is unavailing as to those who have fallen away; ‘for it is impossible,’” etc. His object was not to convert them to the faith, but to confirm and advance them in it.<div eID="gen134308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134309" type="x-p"/>Or the whole argument may be more fully stated thus, — “What I design now to do is not to call you to repentance and faith, to require you to be baptized that you might receive the miraculous gift of the Holy Ghost, and to teach you the doctrine of the resurrection as confirmed by our Savior’s resurrection, and of the day of judgment, when a sentence shall be pronounced on the just and unjust which shall never be reversed; for all these things have been long known to you, and you have made a long profession of them: there is therefore no need of taking such a course, nor is it of any benefit, for if you fall away, it is impossible to restore you again to repentance.” But instead of making the case personal to them, he states it generally. He thus most powerfully stimulated them to make advances in the knowledge of divine truths; for not to advance is to retrograde, and to retrograde is the direct way to apostasy.<div eID="gen134309" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134304"/> <div sID="gen134310"/> <div sID="gen134311" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX T<div eID="gen134311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134312" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 6:5.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the powers of the world to come.</hi> The<hi type="italic"> five </hi>things mentioned here have been variously explained.<div eID="gen134312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1</hi> <hi type="italic">Enlightened,</hi> — baptized, say most of the fathers, and some moderns too, but without any countenance from the use of the word in Scripture, either in the New Testament or in the <hi type="italic">Sept. </hi>It means to emit light, to bring to light, to enlighten, and hence to instruct, to teach. It is often used in the <hi type="italic">Sept. </hi>for a word that means to teach in Hebrew. The taught, the instructed in the duty and necessity of repentance and in Christian truth generally, were no doubt “the enlightened.” This is the meaning given to it by <hi type="italic">Crotius, Beza, Dr</hi> <hi type="italic">Owen, Doddridge, Scott, Stuart, etc.</hi><div eID="gen134313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134314" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2</hi> <hi type="italic">The heavenly</hi> gift, — faith — Christ — the Holy Spirit — pardon of sins — peace of conscience — eternal life: all these have been stated, but the first, “faith towards God,” mentioned in the first verse, is no doubt what is meant.<div eID="gen134314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">Partakers of the Holy Ghost; </hi>that is, in his miraculous powers, as understood by most; it is what is evidently intimated by “baptisms and laying on of hands” in the second verse.<div eID="gen134315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4</hi> <hi type="italic">The good word of God,</hi> — the Gospel — the Gospel covenant — the promises of the Gospel — the heavenly inheritance: such have been the explanations given. There are but two places where the phrase “the good word” occurs, and that is in <reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.29.10">Jeremiah 29:10</reference>, and in <reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.33.14">33:14</reference>; and there it means the promise of restoration given to the Jews, and here it clearly means the promise of the resurrection mentioned in the second verse.<div eID="gen134316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134317" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi> <hi type="italic">The powers of the world to come</hi>; that is, miraculous powers, say most; but αἰω&lt;n oj me&gt;λλων, “the world to come,” says <hi type="italic">Schleusner </hi>never means in the New Testament the time of the Gospel, but the future world. See <reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.12.32">Matthew 12:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.18.30">Luke 18:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.21">Ephesians 1:21</reference>. He therefore explains the clause thus, “The power and efficacy of the doctrine respecting the future felicity of Christians in heaven.” It would have comported more with the “eternal judgment” in these converse, had he said, “respecting the future state both of the saved and of the lost in the next world;” for eternal judgment refers to both.<div eID="gen134317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134318" type="x-p"/>To “taste,” according to the usage of Scripture, is to know, to partake of, to experience, to possess, to enjoy. It does not mean here, as some have thought, slightly to touch a thing, or to sip it, but to know, to know experimentally, to feel, or to enjoy.<div eID="gen134318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134319" type="x-p"/>Thus we see that there is a complete correspondence between the particulars mentioned here and the things stated in verses 1 and 2.<div eID="gen134319" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134310"/> <div sID="gen134320"/> <div sID="gen134321" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX U<div eID="gen134321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134322" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 6: 4­9.</hi> On the subject handled in these verses, <hi type="italic">Stuart </hi>asks and answers a question thus, “Does the whole paragraph pertain to real Christians, or to those who are such only by profession? To the former beyond all reasonable doubt.” The question is not suitable, for the Apostle only speaks of those who had enjoyed certain privileges, and as to whether they were real or merely professing Christians, he does not treat of. Paul addressed the Corinthians as “the Church of God;” and it might in the same way be asked, “Did he address them as real Christians, or as those who were only such by profession t” and it might be answered, “Doubtless as real Christians.” And yet we find that he says, “Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith.” What is spoken of here is the <hi type="italic">enjoyment </hi>of certain privileges and the danger of not making a right use of them, and even the awful doom of those who disregarded them and turned away from the truth.<div eID="gen134322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134323" type="x-p"/>Our author indeed fully admits the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints; but a question of this kind, not relevant to the subject, tends only to create embarrassment. He indeed afterwards somewhat modifies it by saying, that “God treats Christians as free agents and rational beings, and guards them against defection, not by mere <hi type="italic">physical </hi>force, but by <hi type="italic">moral </hi>means adapted to their nature as free and rational agents.” No doubt God thus acts according to the whole current of Scripture; but this in no way contravenes the truth, clearly taught in many passages, that his elect people, real Christians, shall never perish.<div eID="gen134323" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134320"/> <div sID="gen134324"/> <div sID="gen134325" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX X<div eID="gen134325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 6:10.</hi> <hi type="italic">And labor of love, etc</hi> Though <hi type="italic">Griesbach </hi>and others have excluded τοῦ χόπου, “labor,” from the text, yet <hi type="italic">Bloomfield </hi>thinks that there are sufficient reasons for retaining the words. The greatest number of MSS. contain them, and they seem necessary to render the passage complete, though the meaning without them would be the same. There is here an instance of an arrangement similar to what is found often in the Prophets, as will be seen by putting the verse in lines, —<div eID="gen134326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134327" type="x-p"/>“For not unrighteous is God, To forget your work, And the labor of that love Which ye have shewed to his name, Having ministered and ministering to the saints.”<div eID="gen134327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134328" type="x-p"/>Excluding the first line, we see that the first and last are connected, and the two middle lines. Their “work” was to minister to the saints; and in addition to this there was “the labor of that love” which they manifested towards God. He would not forget their work in aiding the saints, nor the love which they had shewn towards his name by an open profession of it, and activity and zeal in God’s service. <hi type="italic">Grotius </hi>says that “the labor of love” was in behalf of the Christian faith.<div eID="gen134328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134329" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Stuart </hi>says that “work” was the outward act, and that “love” was the principle from which it emanated. Examples of this kind no doubt occur often in Scripture, the not being first stated, and then the inward principle or motive; but if “labor” be retained, this view cannot be maintained.<div eID="gen134329" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134324"/> <div sID="gen134330"/> <div sID="gen134331" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX Y<div eID="gen134331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134332" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 6:11.</hi> <hi type="italic">To the full assurance, etc.</hi> The preposition πρὸς, “to,” may be rendered “with regard to, in respect of” If this meaning be given to it, then the diligence required was with reference to the full assurance of hope: they were to exercise diligence in order that they might enjoy the assurance of hope to the end. But if the preposition be rendered “for the sake of,” as by <hi type="italic">Stuart, </hi>then the meaning is, that they were to exercise the same diligence as they had already exhibited in the work and labor of love, for the purpose of attaining the full assurance of hope.<div eID="gen134332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134333" type="x-p"/>Now <hi type="italic">Calvin </hi>takes the first meaning; he considers that the Apostle now refers to the full assurance of hope or of faith as he regards it, as he had before spoken of the works of benevolence. What follows seems to favor this view, for the Apostle proceeds to speak of faith and patience as exemplified by the fathers, especially by Abraham.<div eID="gen134333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134334" type="x-p"/>Some, as <hi type="italic">Beza, </hi>connect “to the end” with “shewing the same diligence,” but it is more suitable to connect them with “the assurance of hope,” as it is done by most.<div eID="gen134334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134335" type="x-p"/>The remarks of <hi type="italic">Scott </hi>on the difference of “the assurance of hope,” of “the understanding,” and of “faith,” are so clear and discriminating that they shall be added, —<div eID="gen134335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134336" type="x-p"/>“He who so understands the Gospel as to perceive the relation of each part to all the rest, and its use as a part of some great design, in something of the same manner that a skillful anatomist understands the use and office of every part of the human body, in relation to the whole, has <hi type="italic">the full assurance of understanding; </hi>and those things willful appear inconsistent, useless, or superfluous to others, he perceives essentially necessary to the system or the great design. The man who is fully convinced that this consistent and harmonious though complicated design is the work and revelation of God, and has no doubt the things testified are true, that the promises and threatenings will be fulfilled, and that Christ will certainly save all true believers, has <hi type="italic">the full assurance of faith, </hi>though he may through misapprehension, or temptation, or other causes, doubt of his own personal interest in this salvation. But he, who beyond doubt or hesitation is assured that he himself is a true believer, interested in all the precious promises, sealed by the sanctifying Spirit, and ‘a partaker of the glory that shall be revealed,’ has <hi type="italic">the full assurance of hope.</hi>”<div eID="gen134336" type="x-p"/><div eID="gen134330"/> <div sID="gen134337"/> <div sID="gen134338" type="x-p"/>APPENDIX Z<div eID="gen134338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen134339" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Chapter 7</hi>:<hi type="bold">14</hi> <hi type="italic"> For under it the people received the Law, etc</hi> These words are variously explained. The preposition ἐπὶ often means “for,” or “on the account of,” as ἐπ᾿ ἐλπίδι, “for the hope,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Acts.26.6">Acts 26:6</reference>;) and so <hi type="italic">Macknight </hi>renders it here “on account of it the people received the Law.” It is not true that the people were under the priesthood when they were subjected to the Law; for the Law was given before the Levitical priesthood was established: it was after the tabernacle was made and set up that Aaron and his sons were consecrated priests. See <reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.40.12-Exod.40.15">Exodus 40:12-15</reference><div eID

                     </ns0:gap>and Judaising Christians had no right to eat of the <ns0:hi>Christian-Altar.</ns0:hi> For a Law of their own excludes them from it, which is written, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 6.30. and 16.27. <ns0:hi>That the Bodies of those living Creatures,</ns0:hi> which were yearly sacrificed, as a Sin-Offering for Priests and Peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, both of the Bull and the He-goat with their Skins, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> were burnt wholly without the Camp; so as neither the Priests, nor any of the People had any part of this Bull or Goat allowed them to eat, having no right to it by the Law of God, which otherwise ordered it.                <ns0:p n="12">12 Wherefore <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Because that Sacrifice for Sin was burnt without the Camp, therefore Jesus to fulfil the Type, suffered without the Gate: and as they might not eat of that Expiatory Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />crifice, so neither of this.                <ns0:p n="24">24 Salute <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">He sends his <ns0:hi>Salutations,</ns0:hi> which were good Wishes and Prayers for the Peace, Prosperity, Health and Happiness of their Souls, and Bodies, and success in all their Concernments, <ns0:hi>first</ns0:hi> unto their excellent <ns0:hi>Guides</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Rulers,</ns0:hi> v. 7, 17. that they may prosper and succeed in their work among the Saints; and then unto the <ns0:hi>Saints</ns0:hi> themselves conveying the Gospel-peace, according to Christ's Command, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 10.12. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 10.5. Which <ns0:hi>Saints</ns0:hi> were all those <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi> dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perst in several places, and there convening, and maintain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing Church-Society; and to whose Hand the Epistle first came they were to receive the Salutations themselves, and transmit them to others, with his own he transmits the Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lutations of all that part of the Church of Christ, which was in <ns0:hi>Italy,</ns0:hi> to them.                <ns0:p n="25">25 Grace <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> with you all.
